stimulus.text: The map shows the four voyages of Christopher Columbus, 1492 to 1504. | Voyage | Years | Main landfalls | | First | 1492 to 1493 | Bahamas, Cuba, Hispaniola | | Second | 1493 to 1496 | Lesser Antilles, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Hispaniola | | Third | 1498 to 1500 | Trinidad and the South American mainland near Venezuela | | Fourth | 1502 to 1504 | Coast of Central America, from Honduras to Panama |
stimulus.source_note: Map by Albert Bushnell Hart, 1906, public domain; voyage dates verified against standard accounts.

source: original; stimulus map from the shared pool, Hart 1906, public domain; voyage dates verified against standard accounts

primary_sources: Hart, map of the four voyages of Columbus (1906)

stem: The map marks a Line of Demarcation running through the Atlantic. What does that line best show about the period?

options.text: The line marks the equator across the middle of the Atlantic.
options.misconception: Confuses a north-south boundary line with the equator, which runs east to west.

options.text: The line traces the route of the first voyage westward.
options.misconception: Treats a boundary line as a voyage route; the routes are the numbered red lines.

options.text: The line marks the border between Spanish and French colonies.
options.misconception: Names the wrong rival; the line divided Spanish and Portuguese claims.

options.text: Spain and Portugal divided their claims to new lands, shaping later colonization.

rationales.general:
1. Find the line on the map. It runs north to south through the Atlantic, apart from the numbered voyage routes.
2. Ask what a line on a map can mark. It can mark a boundary between claims.
3. Read the label on the map. It calls the line the Line of Demarcation of 1493, the papal line drawn 100 leagues west of the Azores and Cape Verde.
4. Conclude. The line shows Spain and Portugal dividing claims to new lands, and the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 later moved that line farther west.
Remember: a straight line on an early map is often a claim, not a coast, so ask who drew it and why.
rationales.A: The equator runs east to west across the map, while the Line of Demarcation runs north to south, so the two are different lines.
rationales.B: The voyage routes are the numbered red lines, while the Line of Demarcation is a separate boundary line.
rationales.C: The line divided Spanish and Portuguese claims under the papal demarcation of 1493, not Spanish and French claims.
rationales.D: The line on the map is the papal Line of Demarcation of 1493, which divided new lands between Spain and Portugal; Tordesillas in 1494 later moved the line farther west.

figures.caption: Map of the four voyages of Christopher Columbus; the map's printed title gives 1492 to 1503, but the fourth voyage returned in 1504
